item.title: How to Disclose Infidelity
item.description:
Across the world, emotional and sexual infidelity destroys relationships, leading to breakups or divorces. In the United States alone, it is estimated that 20-40% of relationships are affected by infidelity (Marín, Christensen, & Atkins, 2014). Emotional and sexual infidelity is damaging because it affects self-esteem, causes depression and anxiety, creates attachment injuries, and triggers suicidal ideation in hurt partners.

Frequently, infidelity in relationships leads to significant distress for both partners, especially in the brief period after disclosure or discovery. Hurt partners react in a variety of ways to discovering infidelity: initial shock, wanting to leave, time apart from the offending partner, feeling trapped with no option to leave, or staying and beginning the work to rebuild the relationship.

The Fact of Disclosure

While the consequences are the same for disclosing infidelity to a hurt partner or the hurt partner discovering infidelity, it seems that gentle and thoughtful disclosure is more likely to lead to repair, recovery, and reconciliation between the partners (Simonyi-Gindele & Simonyi-Gindele, 2020).

Involved partners often believe that disclosing infidelity is the harmful part. However, the infidelity itself does the real damage to the hurt partner (Simonyi-Gindele & Simonyi-Gindele). If the offending partner validates the hurt partner’s sense of reality, the disclosure will go more easily. As described above, the hurt partner will experience a gamut of emotions. Emotionally, hurt partners will feel like their entire world has collapsed around them.

There are a few exceptions to a gentle, thoughtful disclosure. The first exception is when the hurt partner has expressed an imminent, verifiable threat to harm the involved partner if he or she discloses infidelity.

In those special circumstances, preventive law enforcement intervention and involvement would be strongly advised before disclosure. The offending partner may choose to keep it secret or divorce the hurt partner as an alternative. Not disclosing infidelity in these cases leads to superficial emotional intimacy.

The second exception applies to individuals with a sex addiction. Since there are likely multiple sex partners and infidelities, the process is more complex than a simple thoughtful disclosure (Schneder et al., 1998). In addition, the hurt partner is likely aware of the involved partner’s dalliances (Schneder et al.). Individuals with a sex addiction may require advanced mental health care at an inpatient program specializing in sexual addiction and betrayal.

The Process of Disclosure

Schneder and associates concluded that disclosure is often a process, not a one-time event. However, disclosure should not be staggered. It is best to get everything in the open, as described below. Nevertheless, we are human and tend to forget some details, especially if we do not have support to remind us.

Second, they reminded us that the initial disclosure is usually the make-or-break point to healing the relationship in the long run, including all the major elements of the acting-out behaviors. Initial disclosure does not involve the “gory details.” The “gory details” are sexual positions used by the offending and affair partners and anything that enhanced the romance, i.e., perfume, adult toys, and lingerie, between them.

Third, they recommend that both partners need support from professionals and peers during the process of disclosure. When the involved partner chooses to disclose infidelity to his or her partner, it is advisable to gather all the information possible. Although heart-rending, disclosure is best when it delivers everything in one swift and painful blow.

The offending partner must have a support system in place. The support system will keep the involved partner from leaving out any details. Offending partners are often anxious when disclosing information to the hurt partner. For the hurt partner, a support system will help him or her sort his or her feelings objectively, weigh the pros and cons, give the hurt partner the pros and cons, and help guide the recovery process.

Disclosing Details of Infidelity

If details are left out, the disclosure becomes staggered disclosure. Staggered disclosure causes further injury because it rips the scab off a healing wound. Staggered disclosure requires as much work as discovery of infidelity to rebuild trust with the hurt partner. The hurt partner asks him or herself questions, such as “What is next?” “What did my partner leave out?” “Is my partner truly remorseful?” or “Is my partner trying to weasel out of natural and logical consequences?

In addition to a support system, the involved partners need to be prepared to answer all the hurt questions. The most important questions are:

  • who the affair partner was
  • when the affair began and ended
  • how many separate acts of infidelity occurred
  • what made the affair partner different than the hurt partner
  • whether there was safe sex
  • whether the offending partner was in love with the affair partner
  • whether the affair partner and the involved partner were treated for STDs
  • whether contact with the affair partner has ended
  • whether a child was conceived during the affair
  • why the offending partner is choosing to return to the hurt partner

This writer believes that two particular questions are strictly off-limits for the hurt partner to ask: 1) which sex positions were used during the affair, and 2) whether items were used to spice up the affair, i.e., lingerie, perfume, adult toys, etc. Both questions tend to retraumatize hurt partners as they visualize these acts or scenes repeatedly in their minds.

When disclosing infidelity, especially when done without a mental health professional present, disclosure needs to be slow and in bite-sized pieces. The hurt partner will likely be quite hurt and will need time to absorb everything.

Thus, it is advisable to allow a minimum of two to three hours to disclose the infidelity. Allowing plenty of time gives the hurt partner time to absorb the information emotionally and take appropriate breaks to prevent flooding of emotions. It is important to reveal everything in one session.

Considerations When Disclosing Infidelity

When disclosing infidelity, it is important to be empathetic toward the hurt partner. The involved partner must place him or herself in the shoes of the hurt partner. Second, the offending partner must not pass judgment on the hurt partner or minimize his or her actions. Third, the involved partner must recognize all the emotions the hurt partner is experiencing. Fourth, the offending partner must communicate the understanding of the hurt partner’s emotions by validating them.

It is guaranteed that the hurt partner will have some strong emotions. It is wise for the involved partner not to treat the hurt partner’s emotions as an overreaction. Likewise, it would be detrimental to tell the hurt partner how to feel. As described above, the hurt partner will feel blindsided, shocked, confused, grieved, and emotionally kicked in the stomach.

It is unrealistic to believe that forgiveness happens instantaneously, like taking a magic pill that erases all harm done. In cases of infidelity, the offending partner must apologize for the infidelity.

However, it is completely delusional to believe that forgiveness takes place immediately. When infidelity is disclosed, validating the hurt partner’s pain, accepting responsibility, laying out a recovery plan, seeking individual treatment beforehand, and taking steps before disclosing, i.e., switching jobs to move away from an affair partner/co-worker, goes a long way for the hurt partner.

In addition to the three requirements above, trust must be rebuilt. Trust involves honesty, transparency, reliability, and security. Security is the subjective quality of feeling safe. No objective standard can measure security. Reliability means being willing to be held liable again and again. An offending partner in infidelity says something and follows through with it.

Transparency means everything is visible and can be inspected by the hurt partner. The involved partner does not try to hide anything from the hurt partner. Honesty means being truthful, even when it hurts. Deception and manipulation of the hurt partner do not occur.

Regardless of whether the infidelity was disclosed or discovered, the reconciliation process will be excruciating for both partners. Infidelity recovery includes evaluating the damage to the relationship, rebuilding trust, reestablishing commitment between partners, creäting and maintaining accountability, learning to communicate more deeply, and developing true forgiveness (Fife et al., 2023).

Next Steps

Often, when rebuilding a relationship plagued by infidelity, couples require forgiveness and seek professional help. An educated, Christian counselor can teach clients how to forgive each other, help them manage painful and recurring memories, assist the couple with their changing couple-dynamics, and modify power dynamics within their relationship.

At Spokane Christian Counseling, we have many counselors who have walked alongside countless clients to restore relationships and help them start on the path of recovery and reconciliation.

Fife, S. T., Gossner, J. D., Theobald, A., Allen, E., Rivero, A., & Koehl, H. (2023). Couple healing from infidelity: A grounded theory study. Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 40(12), 3882-3905.

Marín, R. A., Christensen, A. & Atkins, D. C. (2014). Infidelity and behavioral couple therapy: Relationship outcomes over 5 years following therapy, Couple and Family Psychology: Research and Practice, 3 (1), 1-12.

Schneider, J. P., Corley, M. D., & Irons, R. K. (1998). Surviving disclosure of infidelity: Results of an international survey of 164 recovering sex addicts and partners. Sexual Addiction & Compulsivity, 5(3), 189–217. https://doi.org/10.1080/10720169808400162

Simonyi-Gindele, C. & Simonyi-Gindele, V. (25 Mar. 2020). Key things to include when disclosing infidelity (Episode 271). The Marriage Podcast for Smart People. Retrieved from Key Things to Include When Disclosing Infidelity – OnlyYouForever

item.title: Learning How to Forgive Yourself When It Feels Impossible
item.description:
It’s easy to hold a grudge against someone who wronged you, but it can also be relatively easy to forgive them. Learning to forgive yourself can be more challenging. Forgiving usually goes something like this:

You replay the offensive action as it unfolded in real-time in your head with a judgmental eye. You speculate about motives and judge them in all their faults and frailties and talk it over with your best friend, who will assure you that you were not at fault (because that’s what best friends do). Eventually, forgiveness and acceptance can come through an apology, bringing restoration to the relationship and satisfaction to your soul.

But when you’re holding resentment against yourself, the act of forgiveness can be more complicated and the process less straightforward. Do you want to confess and regurgitate your transgressions with someone else? And when you’re fighting with yourself, a healing apology may not be forthcoming.

Why It’s Important to Forgive Yourself

Sometimes we’re easy on ourselves, like the time you justified popping a few grapes at the grocery store just to test them. There are other times when we are our own harshest judges. Our self-serving bias may allow us to take credit for our successes (of course they’re a result of my abilities). When it comes to our failures, we may blame those on external factors such as someone else’s actions or even bad luck.

But when we judge our actions with the ferociousness of a chef judging a microwave dinner, we forget that we should also show ourselves grace. Holding yourself to a high standard is commendable, but so is forgiving yourself when you fall short of those goals. After all, even those award-winning chefs have off days and come home to microwave a TV dinner.

We’re allowed to learn and grow and to try again and again without the constraints of self-criticism holding us back.

Viewing yourself through the lens of your mistakes can weigh you down, making even your victories and moments of peace a little less meaningful. When you forgive yourself, you can let go of that weighty guilt and relentless regret. This means you can stop carrying around the weight of your mistakes. Because you know what? God has already promised to forgive you.

Learning to Accept Forgiveness

As a follower of Christ, you know you are called to forgive others, but that same grace and compassion should be extended to yourself. God has already made a way for your forgiveness by sending His only Son to die for your sins. Now, you just have to accept that gift and release yourself from the harshness of your regret.

That process isn’t always easy. In fact, forgiving yourself can be even more difficult than forgiving others and is a deeply personal process. We’ve all been told to “let it go!” But letting go is easier said than done.

Support as You Forgive Yourself

Thankfully, you don’t have to walk the path alone. A Bible-believing therapist can serve as an invaluable ally in this sometimes-tumultuous process. Your therapist can help you break free from the constricting chains of guilt and point you back into the loving and compassionate arms of the Lord. They can also help you uncover the root of your feelings, reframe your thinking, and empower you to move forward through healing and hope, so you don’t stumble back into self-deprecation.

Forgiving yourself means seeing yourself through the lens of God’s everlasting love, not the foggy and scratched lens of sin and regret. God’s grace is much bigger than your failures and much more everlasting than your sins. Regardless of your past failures and mistakes, you can walk in confidence knowing that you are loved and forgiven. Let the therapists at our location help you find that forgiveness. Give our office a call today.

item.title: What Is Infidelity? 3 Steps To Take If You Find Unfaithfulness In Your Life
item.description:
by Marcia Deah

Love is understood, in a historical way, as one of the great human vocations – but its counterspell has always been infidelity. This terrible, terrible betrayal that can tear apart not only another person, not only oneself, but whole families. – Junot Diaz

When I think of the question, what is infidelity? I think of a deep wound that travels through the body and pierces each part that creates the beautiful bonds of fidelity. To truly understand infidelity, you must truly experience fidelity.

So now the question is, what is fidelity? Fidelity is a commitment to steadfastness, loyalty, and faithfulness to the promises created in relationships, particularly romantic partners. It’s a deep level of intimacy that involves not only sex but also emotional faithfulness, relational loyalty, integrity in words and actions, and sexual exclusivity.

Emotional Faithfulness This involves being honest and transparent with your partner. It protects the emotional bonds the partners have created through consistency, communication, and trust. It requires dedication to not form secret or intimate attachments outside the relationship.

Relational Loyalty It involves keeping the promises between you and your partner, showing up consistently and always prioritizing your relationship over temptations and possible distractions.

Integrity in Your Words and Actions This includes always telling the truth, having open and honest communication, no matter how hard it is to say or to hear. You must align your behaviors with your values. You must be trustworthy even when your partner is not around.

Sexual Exclusivity This is exactly how it sounds. Not breaking the physical boundaries you have agreed upon. In monogamous relationships specifically, it is the choice not to engage in sexual or romantic relations with others.

In simplest terms, fidelity is exactly what the scripture tells us. Fidelity is Love. Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful; it does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth. Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. – 1 Corinthians 13: 4-7

When fidelity is broken, we enter the realms of infidelity. Once we are in these waters, it can be like trying to swim in the ocean against the current. If you continue to go against the current, the harder it will be to stay afloat. However, if you start to go with the current, eventually, with intention, with faith, with love, and with the following three steps, you can overcome the depths of infidelity.

Three Steps for the Partner Who Was Unfaithful

Take full ownership without defensiveness

It is natural to be defensive, even when we are in the wrong. Infidelity can only be a factor in a committed and love-filled relationship. If you are reading this article, I guess that betraying your partner was not a proud moment for you. This is why it is important to acknowledge the choices you made and the impact they had on everyone involved.

This means taking full ownership of your behaviors. You cannot minimize your actions. You must eliminate the urge to defend yourself. Avoid statements such as “yes, but…” Taking ownership will require humility and be foundational in the repair of your relationship.

Explore the internal drivers behind the affair

This may be one of the hardest parts of the repair process. Telling your partner, whom you hurt and betrayed, that you felt a void in your relationship. At times, this has absolutely nothing to do with your partner; it may be internal factors. Unfortunately, it is often more than one reason.

Could it be an emotional disconnection? Do you feel that you and your partner are emotionally aligned? Are you avoiding the truth? Are there needs that you have that are being unmet, or vice versa, are there needs that you are not willing to meet? Are there some personal wounds that have not been addressed or not healed? Understanding the “why” is important because then we can fix the issues instead of repeating the same patterns that caused the disruptions.

It is important to understand yourself and what you need to invoke true change and partnership. These are some questions to begin with, but you will need to explore them not only with your partner, but with the assistance of a licensed couples therapist (such as me). A licensed therapist would be beneficial simply for support and guidance, and most importantly, an unbiased perspective.

Offer consistency, transparency, and repair behaviors

Again, this could be achieved with you and your partner; however, counsel from a licensed provider will reap better results. There will be questions that your partner has. You will need to answer them with care and honesty.

Your partner will need a lot of reassurance and gentleness. Showing them that you are reliable will be crucial because you have shown yourself unreliable with their heart. Being empathetic will go a long way toward re-earning your partner’s trust and regaining clarity.

3 Steps for the Partner Who Discovered the Affair

Stabilize your internal world

You have just been hit with a big fat boot to the chest. The air in your lungs has been snatched from your body suddenly, and now you are expected to breathe anyway. It feels unfair, and it is! You made a commitment to your partner, and they broke your agreement. So, before you can begin to understand what caused the rupture, you must first slow down your nervous system and stabilize your emotions.

Utilize grounding techniques and learn how to breathe steadily again. Utilize healthy coping skills that will assist you in working through the infidelity. Try journaling your journey so that you can recognize where you are healing and where you need more work. Talk it out with someone you trust but be careful with this option as it can have repercussions. Your goal needs to be clarity, so you have to work on reducing reactivity as much as possible.

Identify what you need to feel safe

Remember safety is always the top priority and the backbone of the operation. Without felt safety, you will not be able to work through anything. Your emotional safety will require honesty, transparency, and reassurance from your partner. Identifying your physical safety will mean holding on to your space, your boundaries, and even your routines.

A big part will also be relational safety. You will want to know the whys and, at times, certain details. Understand that some details are unnecessary to know. Knowing certain details can be more detrimental than just leaving it be. When you can identify your needs, this will help calm some of the chaos.

Express your experience without self-blame

With your partner, share the impact their behaviors have on you and your relationship. Avoid further accusations while remaining true to how the actual betrayal has affected you. When you can talk through these hurts with your partner, it helps you reclaim your voice and helps the relationship move forward positively toward repairing.

Three Steps for Healing as a Couple

Rebuild safety together

As stated above, the relationship will need the restoration of emotional stability. This will look like creating predictable routines and communication with one another. Sometimes this may entail overly communicating with your partner until trust is restored. You will need to practice being transparent with one another, so you do not feel the need to babysit your partner’s every move. It is not fair to you, them, or the relationship.

It does not create a sense of stability; it creates surveillance. You need to agree on boundaries that will help you both feel grounded and supported. Remember that even though betrayal is the reason you are in this situation, there were still underlying factors that contributed to this.

So, slow down, allow the conflict to settle through your hard work, and do not overwhelm yourselves. Think of safety as your soil. Without your safety, nothing will grow. Read my article on forgiveness because this will also play a major factor in your safety.

Rebuild understanding through honest dialogue

Since you have safety as your soil, and forgiveness as your fertilizer, you have already begun the growth process. Since you are doing the work to grow, you can now make meaning of what has happened. In this step, you will practice sharing your emotions without attacking each other (easier said than done).

The best way to do this is to listen with an ear for understanding, not to defend yourself or your behavior. As hard as it will be, you must seek to understand not only the impact, but also the unmet needs on both ends. In therapy, we can work on your relationship narrative. What was the relationship before, what is it now, what do you see it as in the future?

Understanding your story will help reduce confusion, resentment, and assumptions in your relationship. You will begin to see the full picture rather being stuck in your own hurt, story, guilt, shame, or unforgiveness.

Rebuild connection through intentional repair

In this step, you will create a new relationship – the final draft. This will not be your story moving forward. It will be a chapter of your past. You will need to practice consistency with your partner. Be determined to repair using some of the skills I mentioned above, such as empathy, reassurance, accountability, honesty, openness, forgiveness, etc.

It will also be helpful to rebuild your trust through small, steady, and reliable action steps. Relationships thrive from intimacy. Yes, you will have to be intimate with your partner again. You have to be willing to be vulnerable for real change to take place in your lives. You will have to intentionally re-establish emotional intimacy and even physical intimacy.

You will need to create goals and shared meaning. What is your vision for the relationship, and how can you create rituals or routines to ensure your healthy relationship? Your healing is not about the old relationship; it’s about building a new, stronger, safer, and more connected relationship than ever before.

These last three steps happen simultaneously with the previous steps. You can heal; your relationship is not only survivable, but it is capable of pure, undeniable happiness and love. I would love to be the therapist you choose to help you through this fragile time in your relationship. Book a session with me and let’s work toward rebuilding your connection together.

item.title: Addressing Sexual Intimacy Issues in Marriage
item.description:
Sexual intimacy issues in marriage can stem from many factors. The good news is that it is never too late to rebuild emotional and physical intimacy through communication, reduced performance expectations, and counseling.

Common Sexual Intimacy Issues

Sexual intimacy issues can create a distance physically and emotionally in a marriage. It can lead to hurt, frustration, anger, and resentment. Keeping lines of communication open, being willing to be vulnerable, and seeking help when needed can strengthen the relationship.

The following are several common sexual intimacy issues couples face.

Hormonal Changes

Hormonal changes throughout life can lead to decreased libido or a mismatched libido between a couple. For example, a woman going through early menopause symptoms may have a lower libido as well as physical symptoms, such as vaginal dryness, that make sex painful. While her husband may have higher hormone levels, causing him to want to make love more often.

Hormonal changes are normal. If they become a problem where sexual intimacy is concerned, speak to your physician about the possibility of hormone therapy.

Lack of Emotional Intimacy

Expecting physical intimacy without emotional intimacy can lead to lulls in a marriage. The act of sex becomes more of a demand than a pleasure, losing the connection it once held. Emotional intimacy starts with non-sexual acts of love. For example, little acts like holding hands, brushing by the other, maintaining eye contact, and spending quality time together all build emotional intimacy.

Consider scheduling weekly or bi-weekly date nights and make it a priority to touch your spouse more. Put in the effort to serve and spoil your spouse in the little things. Open the line of communication by asking for the same in return.

After Effects of Infidelity

Infidelity can tear a relationship apart. If you are working on rebuilding your marriage after infidelity or an affair, know that it is possible with time, effort, forgiveness, and grace from the Lord. The after-effects of infidelity can make it more challenging for spouses to express themselves sexually as they have lost the trust and freedom that makes sexual intimacy safe in marriage.

Speak to a counselor about ways to rebuild your marriage after infidelity. Couples therapy is effective in getting spouses on the same page.

Medical Conditions

Certain medical conditions and side effects of medications can lead to sexual intimacy issues in marriage. For example, a man can experience erectile dysfunction at any age, while a woman may feel overwhelmed by family responsibilities while dealing with hormonal changes and anxiety. Combined, these issues can decrease libido.

Speak to your physician about medical conditions and medications hampering your sexual relationship and work on building and strengthening emotional intimacy during this season.

Meeting an “Obligation”

No one feels like having sex all the time, especially if you are tired, anxious, depressed, or ill. Often, spouses will participate to keep the peace, but it feels more like an obligation than a connection. This can lead to bitterness, resentment, and frustration.

If meeting an obligation has become more of the norm, speak to a counselor today about how to get both of you back on track and address the issues holding you back.

Christian Counseling for Sexual Intimacy Issues in Marriage

Christian counseling combines faith-based principles with evidence-based techniques to address the individual holistically. When it comes to sexual intimacy issues, your counselor will help you work on communication, build emotional intimacy, seek treatment for medical conditions, and learn to lean into each other in this season while drawing closer to God. Contact us today to get started.

item.title: Anxiety in the Bible: How to Move from Worry Toward Rest
item.description:
We often try to ground our sense of peace in things that can change in an instant. We look to our health, financial stability, our friendships and other relationships, our looks, and other areas for peace. These things can have benefits in their own way, but they ultimately form a poor foundation for life because they aren’t permanent.

If we want something that will stand the test of time, a foundation upon which to build our lives that will survive the fiercest assaults that life can launch against us, such a hope and such a foundation can only be found in Jesus. This has remarkable implications for our lives, including the sense of security we can have, knowing that we are safe in Christ, even when we go through tough times.

Anxiety is a normal reaction to stress as a potential danger. We need a way to protect ourselves against harm, and so our bodies have the remarkable ability to prepare for such instances. Our fight-or-flight response, which is triggered by stress and danger (whether real or imagined), prepares our body to respond appropriately to the situation. This could be a job interview, a first date, or a snake that just slithered across your path.

While feeling a bit of anxiety can be a normal response in stressful situations, such as a public speaking engagement or taking a test, those feelings of anxiety can also function as an indicator of something deeper. It’s important to notice when they become excessive, all-consuming, and begin interfering with your day-to-day life. In those cases, anxiety has become a disorder, and that is a condition diagnosable by a mental health professional.

If you find that your anxiety is out of control and undermining your well-being and daily functioning, you should consider going to a mental health professional for a proper diagnosis.

Thankfully, the Lord has not left us without wisdom and guidance regarding anxiety or any other part of our lives. Treatment for anxiety includes psychotherapy and medication. Part of what happens in psychotherapy is talking with your therapist. They can help you begin understanding the causes of anxiety, your triggers for anxiety, and any patterns of thought, behavior, and action that undermine your well-being.

These unhealthy and unhelpful patterns of behavior and thinking need to be understood and ultimately replaced by healthier ones. Part of how you can deal with everyday anxiety, as well as deeper anxiety disorders, is to speak God’s truths over yourself. You can begin to pattern your thinking and being in ways that align with God’s truth and ways.

Below are some Scriptures that can help us work through our anxiety and ground us in the hope, security, and freedom from fear that can only come through Jesus Christ.

Come and find rest

“Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” – Matthew 11:28–30, ESV

Jesus invites people to place their trust in him and place their lives in his hands. For those who are carrying the burden of religious legalism, Jesus invites you to set it down. Instead of being weighed down by the laws that seemed to multiply guilt without necessarily offering any relief, Jesus offers rest for our souls.

This means that He is offering freedom from the crushing burden of guilt of trying to earn salvation by good works to those who desire eternal rest and seek forgiveness of their sins.

Sometimes, we are anxious in life because we feel like we don’t measure up to a standard, whether it is that of the people around us or to God’s standards. Jesus frees us from that by offering us the lighter burden of being his disciples and finding rest through simple commitment to him.

We live for Him, and He loves, cares for, and accepts us already. We pursue our life in Him from the position of knowing we are already loved and accepted, and we don’t have to earn it because Jesus has done it for us on the cross.

When good things become ultimate things that take us off course, it can make us anxious as we try to keep it all together. In our culture, we are consumed by many anxieties and concerns, and these have become ultimate for many of us. When things like our safety, our personal health, or the environment and its viability become ultimate concerns, the enormity of the problems, coupled with our limited capacities, makes us feel endlessly fragile and anxious.

What we need is to bring things back into perspective and make God the center of our lives. That way, these other things begin to occupy their proper place. When we yield to Jesus and his yoke, it allows us to approach these good concerns with the resources and wisdom of God, and that can help us find peace and rest. We can trust that our work in the Lord will not be in vain (1 Corinthians 15: 58). We don’t need to feel anxious about our impact or how things will unfold.

Finding Peace in Hard Places

The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul. He leads me in paths of righteousness for his name’s sake. Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil,
for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me. – Psalm 23:1-4, ESV

Fear is probably the strongest human emotion, and we often agonize over all the challenging and dreadful things that could happen to us at any moment. This includes what might happen to our health and finances, losing our loved ones, failing at something important, or being rejected.

Life is often not safe, and we never know what we can find in the hard things we go through. Many things can bring suspense and danger in our lives. These verses from Psalm 23 are a good reminder that the people of God have assurance that God is with them in those times, and so they need not fear. God draws us to find rest and restoration when we follow and trust him.

Trusting In God’s Provision and Care

And he said to his disciples, “Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will put on. For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing.

“Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Of how much more value are you than the birds! And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? If then you are not able to do as small a thing as that, why are you anxious about the rest?” –  Luke 12:22-26, ESV

There are many reasons why believers should not be anxious, and several of them are given in this passage from Luke. For one thing, our lives are more than what we eat; even our bodies are more than what we eat. We do need food and clothing, but these things enable us to focus on what life is really about: loving God and loving our neighbor. It’s challenging, but we can love God and our neighbor whether we are well-fed or not.

If our lives are preoccupied by the means and not the ends of our lives, we can be consumed by the pressure to gather the things that seemingly secure our existence, so much so that we miss the point. Believers also shouldn’t be anxious because they realize how much value they possess in God’s eyes. If he cares for birds, why wouldn’t he care for you?

Anxiety is also not in our best interests because none of us has enough control over our own life, even to add a single hour to our span of life. It’s quite counterintuitive, but striving and taking things into our own hands, and then getting anxious because life is not under our control, doesn’t help us. It is far better to surrender ourselves to the loving care of our heavenly Father, who does have everything under control.

Important Reminders

Psalm 56 reminds us that “When I am afraid, I put my trust in you.” (Psalm 56:3, NIV) We can try to put our trust elsewhere, but those things will ultimately fail and disappoint us. This will likely lead us into deeper anxiety and worry as we try to secure ourselves against the hardships we face in life.

Writing nearly seventeen centuries ago, in his long prayer called Confessions, Augustine wrote, “You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our hearts are restless until they rest in you.” (Augustine) Our restless and anxious hearts try to find peace and rest in many ways, but we can only find what we are looking for in the Lord. This is our deepest need.

To deal with our anxiety, we should be aware of this need and where to have it met. We can grow in our awareness of our unhealthy patterns of behavior and thought through therapy and with the assistance, when necessary, of medication to ease the symptoms of anxiety. This can help us function in life. If you’re ready to learn more about therapy for anxiety, contact this office for more information.

The post Anxiety in the Bible: How to Move from Worry Toward Rest appeared first on Spokane Christian Counseling.

item.title: Is it Justified Guilt or Shame?
item.description:
Guilt and shame have been a part of the human experience from the dawn of man. After both Eve and Adam ate the fruit in the Garden of Eden, one of the first emotions they felt was described as what we know today as shame. “Then the eyes of both of them were opened, and they realized they were naked; so they sewed fig leaves together and made coverings for themselves.” (Genesis 3:7, NIV) Because sin entered the world, they became self-aware and felt ashamed.

Guilt in the Bible is connected to specific actions or sins. It’s the awareness that you have done something wrong, which leads to repentance and corrective action. An example of this can be found in Psalm 51 when David expresses guilt for his specific wrongdoings and seeks restoration.

Guilt is meant to signal to us that we may have done something wrong, disappointed God, or let someone else down. In small doses, guilt can be helpful because it encourages us to pause to analyze our behavior, take accountability, and correct our behavior.

Shame, however, works differently. While guilt focuses on behavior, shame targets identity. Guilt tells you that you did something wrong, while shame tells you that something is wrong with you. This is an important distinction because guilt can lead to growth, but shame leads to hiding and self-condemnation.

For some people, guilt is more than a fleeting feeling or a minor emotional response. Instead, it can become a default emotional state or a lens through which they view themselves and the world, and can lead to chronic shame.

This pattern can be both exhausting and deeply frustrating. Why do some people default to guilt? Is it linked to Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)? Does it relate to other negative emotions? Or is it rooted in learned patterns from early life experiences?

Let’s explore the complex interplay of ADHD, emotional regulation, cognitive biases, and environmental factors that can lead someone to habitually default to guilt. Most importantly, let’s learn how to break the cycle.

Understanding Guilt

Before diving deep into why someone might default to guilt, it’s important to define the emotion itself. Guilt is an internal signal that arises when a person believes they have violated a moral, social, or personal standard or have violated God’s law. It focuses on behavior.

It tells you that “I did something wrong.” Shame, however, focuses on self or “I am a bad person.” While guilt can motivate actions, chronic guilt can create anxiety, depression, and a sense of inadequacy.

Defaulting to guilt means that you tend to immediately assume responsibility for negative outcomes, even when the situation is minor, ambiguous, or not entirely in your control. Your brain has a preset mode of sorts. Any mistake, conflict, or unmet expectation triggers guilt automatically.

ADHD and the Guilt Loop

For many people with ADHD, guilt becomes an almost automatic reaction. ADHD affects executive functioning, which includes planning, prioritizing, remembering tasks, and managing time. When these systems don’t work smoothly, it’s easy to forget responsibility, miss deadlines, and overlook details.

Some people with ADHD may feel an overwhelming guilt in response to their failures, even if they didn’t intend to fail. This happens because people with ADHD have brains that amplify errors and then ruminate on them.

Emotional regulation, another area often impacted by ADHD, makes it difficult to step back from feelings of guilt. A minor oversight can quickly spiral into a cycle of self-condemnation. This is where guilt feeds anxiety, shame, and even physical tension.

Other negative emotions can feel like guilt

Anyone, even those without ADHD, can have guilt as a default emotion out of a pattern or habit. Any negative emotion that they feel, from embarrassment to unmet expectations, can manifest itself as guilt. That’s because guilt rarely exists in isolation but often intertwines with shame, anxiety, and low self-esteem.

When guilt escalates, it can morph into shame. It can feel crushing and can affect your self-image. If you’re already experiencing low self-esteem, guilt will be amplified. Soon, you believe that every misstep is a confirmation of your personal inadequacies.

Anxiety can also contribute to default guilt. When anxiety is present, the mind constantly scans for what might go wrong or what could have been done better. Instead of evaluating a situation realistically, the anxious brain jumps straight to self-blame. You might find yourself apologizing excessively, replaying conversations, or assuming responsibility for other people’s emotions.

Learned Guilt and Responsibility

Default guilt is often learned early in childhood as a way to survive emotionally, relationally, or even spiritually. When a child grows up in an environment where mistakes are exaggerated or their emotional needs are dismissed, they often start to feel a deep sense of guilt.

If a child’s behavior dictates whether or not there’s harmony in the house, they will see each bad behavior as a catastrophic mistake, and guilt then becomes a protective strategy. This guilt becomes their automatic response to every mistake made, even when guilt isn’t warranted.

Children with ADHD are particularly vulnerable to this pattern. Because their behavior is often corrected more frequently, misunderstood, or labeled as careless or disruptive, they may internalize the belief that they’re always the problem. This repeated feedback trains their brain to assume fault automatically. Guilt becomes much less about what actually happened and more about their attempts to prevent future disapproval.

In Christian homes, this pattern can become even more prevalent because it’s often unintentionally reinforced. When obedience is emphasized without equal attention to grace, a sensitive or neurodivergent child may confuse spiritual growth with emotional self-punishment.

In these situations, a child learns to monitor themselves constantly, searching for what they did wrong rather than resting and relying on God’s grace. Conviction then leads to self-shame instead of repentance and restoration.

Therapeutic Help

It’s important to be able to distinguish between justified guilt and shame. For people who live with ADHD or long-standing emotional patterns, default guilt can become a part of their life and can undermine their self-esteem and even their spiritual health.

If guilt has become a learned or neurological response that has developed to cope or avoid conflict, you may benefit from working with a licensed therapist. A trained professional understands emotional patterns and neurological differences from a biblical perspective.

ADHD informed therapists recognize that chronic guilt is how the brain might process mistakes, expectations, and emotional feedback. A therapist will help you work through this automatic guilt response and provide you with practical tools for emotional regulation. They will teach you how to do more realistic self-assessments, which are often more difficult for people with ADHD.

Therapy can help you figure out where justified guilt is serving its intended purpose of growth, and where it becomes misplaced or excessive. You will learn to recognize your automatic guilt responses. You’ll also learn how to challenge these ideas so you respond to mistakes, emotions, and relational interactions with appropriate and healthy responses. Through this process, you will be able to use guilt as the tool it’s intended to be rather than a constant condemnation.

A Christian therapist will also use a biblical base to remind you that God’s correction is rooted in His love for us. It is not to keep you in a state of depression or anxiety. Guilt is meant to convict, not cause internalized shame.

God’s correction is specific, loving, and restorative. Shame is vague, consistent, and condemning. In therapy, you will learn to quiet the constant voice of misplaced guilt and shame so that the loving voice of God can speak truth into your life.

Living in Freedom

Healing from default guilt will give you a tremendous sense of freedom. You shouldn’t lower your standards or avoid responsibility to achieve that goal, but rather use guilt to form your spiritual and moral boundaries. When you break free of the guilt loop, you will begin to relate to yourself with the same grace that God extends to you.

You can start this process with a Christian therapist on this site. Reach out to the reception office to connect with someone who can help you find freedom from shame.

The post Is it Justified Guilt or Shame? appeared first on Texas Christian Counseling.

item.title: 3 Life Stages When Female Friendships Are Essential
item.description:
Female friendships can be complicated to maintain, tough to build, and even more challenging to restore when there’s a break. It might feel frustrating or pointless to continue putting the work into these relationships. But as you grow and change through life’s seasons, your friends are the ones who sustain you and remind you of your purpose.

Here are five life stages when female friendships aren’t just nice to have but are empowering and essential.

Transitioning into Teen Years with Friendship

This life stage can be fraught with drama, disagreements, and simply changing your mind about so many topics. However, when transitioning from childhood and early adolescence to the teen years, having female friendships for support is integral to emotional and mental health.

When you were 12, 13, or 14, what were you most concerned with? Was it makeup, beauty products, clothing, shoes, or boys? If your answer is yes, you’re in like company. Many young women entering their teen years think about these, too. However, did you know that teen girls today also have deeper, heavier worries on their minds?

Recent research suggests that teen girls are also concerned about long-term decisions, such as where they’ll attend college, what career to pursue, how they’ll earn an income, and family conflict resolution. Just as with adult females, this life stage is one where, without supportive friends, a young teen may find it even more challenging to navigate than it already is.

So, how do teen girls form supportive, healthy female friendships? First, they look to their role models. Many teens learn how to treat friends by the way their parents treat others. If you’re the mother of a teen girl, remember that she’s watching and listening to how you talk to, treat, and talk about your own friends.

Second, pay attention to how your daughter talks about casual friends at school. If one day there’s a breakup, and the next day there’s a hookup between her bestie and her bestie’s boyfriend, it might mean her best girl is prone to drama, mixed signals, or a preoccupation with the things that aren’t lasting. Listening first and asking questions second about your daughter’s friends is one way to tiptoe into discovering what kinds of people she’s around most.

Most teens spend the majority of their time at school, so it’s normal to be lumped together with people you might not ordinarily choose. Much like an office setting where you can’t choose your co-workers, the same goes for school. That’s why asking questions is vital. Not every friend your daughter talks about is going to be her best one, or healthy, and that’s okay. It’s to be expected.

Letting your daughter in on some friendship secrets could help her as she searches for friends who will guard her vulnerability and add joy to her life rather than drama. Secrets you probably didn’t know you had tucked away might include the power of observation.

Talk to your daughter about things like observing how a friend talks about others and paying attention to her discussions around faith or morality. Also, note whether she’s inclined to persevere when something difficult happens or when she’s tasked with a group project. It’s even important to teach her to recognize if a friend asks for help from trustworthy adults if she’s struggling. Remind your daughter to look for good character in her friends.

Another secret you help her learn is to join teams and activities based on interest level and based on who’s involved. As your daughter decides what activities to pursue, remind her that an activity may not be worth pursuing if it means joining a group of girls who go out after a game to party or who talk about others in a demeaning way.

Sometimes teens need to learn the hard way who a good friend is and isn’t. Having an understanding, listening ear is always a gift to her during this season.

Friendships in Young Adulthood

Whether you see young adulthood as 18 or 25, having female friendships can buoy you during these transitional years.

Women face monumental decisions such as where to live, what career to pursue, and how to find a faith community and grow in their spiritual life. This is also the time when many young women start to reflect on their childhood, see some areas for improvement, and desire a closer relationship with family members.

It can be a terrific time to pursue counseling, too. If you or someone you know has been thinking or talking about family relationships or childhood wounds, our offices are widespread and staffed with credentialed, competent counselors, and we’ll match you with the right person to suit your needs.

Female friendships in your early to mid-20s can be tough to maintain when so many women are in life transitions. Whether they’re getting married, starting a career, pursuing a post-graduate degree, or having children, women during this life stage may find it hard to be consistent with their old friends and carve out time to make new ones.

Some tips we want to remind young women are that they have a unique personality and gifts to share. Old ways of connecting, like community service, are sometimes overlooked unless you’re heavily plugged into a service-oriented church.

Aside from contributing your time or talents to a cause you believe in, community service is also a wonderful way to form female friendships. Look for causes that matter to you, and you’ll likely find others who have at least one interest in common.

Another way to find or maintain female friendships at this stage is to develop a creative communication method that works most of the time. This isn’t the time to wish your friend a casual “let’s keep in touch” or “let’s get together next month.” If you want to maintain friendships, you’ll have to be direct, intentional, targeted, decisive, and a little creative.

Use apps like Marco Polo or WhatsApp to help you stay in touch with regular video chat exchanges or life update check-ins. Arrange to talk regularly and create a Zoom call where you can agree on a set time period (not to cut each other off but to respect each other’s time and commitments during this life stage).

Think about a friend who is getting married. Her life is changing radically, so she might not be able to predict what her everyday life will look like after marriage. But give her a month or so, and then try to connect at a time that works for her. You can mutually decide how often you want to call or text to check in and how you plan to maintain your friendship in a season where your lives may not align.

Consider all that you do have in common and don’t write her off simply because her life stage will shift. She’s going to need a friend who knew her before her marriage and can remind her who she is on tough days. And you’ll benefit from getting insider info on what it’s like to be married. Everything she goes through while adjusting is something you can file away and learn from in the future.

Friendships When Your Children Are Grown and on Their Own

You may be newly empty-nested or empty-nested for a decade, but somewhere in this life stage, friends are going to come in handy. Here’s why.

Being suddenly empty can shock our systems. For some of us, it’s an easy transition at first. But then, after years of watching our adult children make choices on career, life, and love, we may encounter a time when our needs fade into the background of their thriving, busy lives.

It’s not that you aren’t happy that they are doing so well (you are!), but when their lives get chaotic, fruitful, stressful, and full, it’s common for them to forget to include a parent in their world. That’s if you’re close geographically; it’s even harder when you live far away.

Friends can be the balm to your loneliness and feeling left out because they can help you find new interests, explore ideas you’ve never considered before, or take risks that you once would have balked at. Now you have the time, energy, and financial resources to pursue them.

They can also listen when you feel left out, give you a kick in the pants when you need to be reminded you’re not a victim, and help you learn how to be vulnerable when it’s the last thing you want to be.

If you’re newly empty-nested, a friend who stays beside you regardless of her life stage is a treasure. She may not be able to relate to what you are going through, but she can mirror what she sees in you and echo what she hears you say. Having female friendships where we’re heard, seen, and known can carry you through just about anything.

You can carry someone else through this life stage, too. Here’s how:

  • Call and invite her for coffee or a walk, even if she says no too many times. (Don’t give up.)
  • Show up at her house with a to-go coffee from her favorite cafe, chicken salad and croissants, or a puzzle you can work on together. It reminds her that she still has needs and interests outside of her children.
  • Engage in her stories about her children, even if you’ve heard similar ones. Listening to her is a way of holding space for her grief, joy, pain, and the immense transition she’s going through right now.
  • Ask her to try something new with you, somewhere new together. Trying something you’ve never done together builds camaraderie in a way that old hobbies can’t. You’ll probably have to be brave together, and it’ll elicit some laughs, giving your grieving friend a place to escape for a little while.
  • Encourage your friend to attend counseling. Even if it’s just a few sessions, seeing a counselor during seasons of transition can provide her with healthy tools and mindset shifts.

To schedule an appointment with me or one of the other counselors in our online directory, contact our reception team today at Vancouver Christian Counseling in Washington state.

The post 3 Life Stages When Female Friendships Are Essential appeared first on Seattle Christian Counseling.

item.title: Trauma Response: Is it Exhaustion or the Beginning of Faith?
item.description:
If you’ve been through a traumatic experience, you probably have also experienced the exhaustion that comes from the aftermath. Common trauma response symptoms include anxiety, depression, catastrophic thinking, anger, self-blame, hypervigilance, and dissociation, among others.

There comes a point when the burden gets too heavy, and you simply can’t carry it any longer. Some people view this “I just can’t do it anymore” pinnacle as a breaking point, but what if it is actually where your faith begins?

Common Trauma Response Symptoms

A person’s trauma response is experienced in various ways. Perhaps you’ve suffered through a prolonged illness, been a caregiver, gotten divorced, been laid off, or are/were the victim of abuse.

Your body and brain will take these trauma experiences and mull them over, and these significant events in your life will manifest in a variety of ways, depending on a lot of factors. This includes but is not limited to your personal history, the circumstances of the event, and your level of support.

No matter the trauma experience or the initial response, there’s no denying that going through a major life-altering event or taxing season will take its toll on you. Some people cycle through the stages of grief and their trauma response quickly, but for some, the weight of it all can drag them down for a long time.

When It’s Too Much

Dark response seasons can morph into your new normal. Your once trusting heart can suddenly become skeptical because of a betrayal. Your once carefree spirit might suddenly feel the weight of living within a tight budget, and as a result, can develop into a fear of homelessness or bankruptcy that can affect you even months, years, or decades after you’ve landed a new job and have found financial stability.

Trauma experiences change us. Sometimes for the worse, which are the effects that bother us the most and get the most attention. When something happens that not only changes our outlook but seems to rewrite our DNA, it is bound to get more attention than the joy of finding a new job or a compliment we receive.

These changes in our being can feel like protection. We might view our new conservative spending habits as being frugal or good stewards. We might find our caution in relationships as wisdom instead of a response to a toxic friendship. And sometimes we’re right. Sometimes trauma changes who we are and how we respond for the better, or at least not for the worse.

But sometimes, in the darkness of the night, as you struggle to find peace and quiet, even in the comfort of your bed, you can feel the weight of the trauma. Maybe you feel as if you’ve gotten over the original trauma, but those aftereffects, those changes in your thought patterns, or those new insecurities that have cropped up, can exhaust you.

In those moments, you might think to give up. You might just want it all to go away or to find a way to leave it all behind. You might long for that trusting, naïve version of yourself that was kidnapped and replaced with this new cynic. This new anxiety-ridden, socially awkward, and paralyzed shell may seem like an improved version of yourself, one that will protect itself with ten-foot-high brick walls and barbed wire.

But maybe, in those quiet, solitary, undistracted moments, you miss that confident person you used to be or the innocence that was stolen. And it is then that the trauma and consequences culminate and leave you confused, overwhelmed, and simply exhausted.

Is it exhaustion or faith?

Could it be both? When you finally reach your threshold, the pinnacle of the aftereffects, a new thing starts to happen. When you’re at your lowest, and you realize that you’ve hit rock bottom, something inside of you might start to change or emerge.

Amid those overwhelming feelings comes peace knowing you can’t fight anymore. Amidst the exhaustion comes the comforting thought that maybe the fight isn’t even worth it. And in those moments of sheer hopelessness comes the opportunity for faith.

The Bible says clearly, “And we know that in all things God works for the good of those who love Him, who have been called according to His purpose.” (Romans 8:28, NIV) This means that God can bring something meaningful, positive, or redemptive out of even the most painful experiences in your life, if you love Him and are called according to His plan.

God doesn’t waste our pain. Even in our deepest holes, darkest hours, and lowest valleys, God can transform those moments, and us, into something quite beautiful.

Surrender

If you really dissect what is going on, you might start to view your exhaustion and oppression as surrender, not the weakness that you’ve accused yourself of for so long. When you’re wringing your hands and listening to your heartbeat accelerate, maybe you’re finally ready to just give it over, everything, to God.

There is power in giving up your power. Releasing your illusion of control can afford you a great deal of freedom. Yes, you have free will, but as a Christ follower, you also have the vested interest of the Creator who not only can help you but wants to.

When you’ve come to the end of your strength, faith begins. In 2 Corinthians 12, we are given a glimpse into the Apostle Paul’s own suffering:

But He said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Therefore, I will boast all the more gladly about my weakness so that Christ’s power may rest in me. That is why, for Christ’s sake, I delight in weakness, in insult, in hardships, in persecutions, in difficulties. For when I am weak, then I am strong. – 2 Corinthians 12:9-10, NIV

Your exhaustion, overload, and feeling fed up don’t preclude you from God’s grace. In fact, it can be the place where His strength can shine its brightest. It’s the origin of your acknowledgement of your human condition. It is the beginning of you being able to say, “I give up and give it to you, God.” And it’s the start of something amazing.

When your burden becomes knee-buckling, you start to see that your wisdom is finite, your body human, and your reasoning flawed. But it’s also the place where you can more clearly see that God’s wisdom is infinite, His strength enduring, and His reasoning omnipotent.

A Little Help from a Friend

While God can do miraculous healing in the heart and change circumstances to your favor, even in ways you hadn’t thought of yet, He often works through people. In this mindset, Christian therapy can be viewed as a vessel of God’s providential care.

Talking with a skilled Christian therapist can help you identify your trauma and responses. It can give you the chance to dwell in the areas that might be too prickly to dwell in alone. A therapist can also guide you through healthy coping skills and help you reframe your thoughts through a biblical lens. They can walk with you as you process the pain in a safe and supportive environment.

Christian therapy isn’t necessarily meant to fix you instantly, but instead to direct you by helping you understand your story. More importantly, it encourages you to invite God into every messy, complicated chapter.

If you’re exhausted from the aftereffects of trauma, God may be telling you it’s time He steps in and begins to renew your mind. Lean on the power of the Almighty, loving, living God. Consider every hard feeling you have as an arrow, pointing you to the rest, trust, and healing that can only be found in the arms of your loving Father. Are you ready to move from exhaustion to faith? Contact our reception team to schedule an appointment with me or to learn more.

The post Trauma Response: Is it Exhaustion or the Beginning of Faith? appeared first on San Diego Christian Counseling.

item.title: Cultivating Female Friendships in a Small Group
item.description:
Ministry in the modern world might look quite different from what it did in Jesus’ day. We don’t ride donkeys on the way to synagogue or have Jesus with us in the flesh. Even though the world looks different, we can still use biblical principles and Jesus’ example to guide us in ministering to others effectively.

If you’re in a women’s ministry or are a small group or Bible study leader, you’re likely longing to see more than just polite conversation and surface-level connection in your group.

Jesus aimed for that too. He ministered to crowds, but He invested deeply in a small group of disciples. Within that circle, genuine friendship, accountability, and love took root. As a leader, you’re invited to follow His example and create a place where women can experience the same type of safe and authentic connections.

Love and Inclusiveness

And let us consider how we may spur one another on toward love and good deeds… – Hebrews 10:24, NIV

Christian friendship is ultimately the continual act of helping each other grow closer to Jesus. The foundation of Christianity is love, as seen in Jesus’ ultimate sacrifice. And when you approach your ministry with the same spirit of love, you will see fruit. When you model the action of love as a leader, you will begin to see that same spirit manifest in the members of your group because love is contagious.

Praying together regularly with intention is a great way to model love. Prayer not only invites the presence of God into your relationships but also encourages transparency and empathy among participants.

Not everyone will be at the same place in their spiritual life, so be sensitive to those who might not feel comfortable praying aloud. The same goes for Scripture reading. Many people, even good readers, struggle with reading in front of others. Feel free to ask for volunteers, but as a leader, be prepared to read the Scriptures yourself.

Practicing patience is another way to ensure that your group is full of love and acceptance. While you might not get an ideal blend of personalities in your group, keep in mind that the purpose is to learn how to love people who are vastly different from us. This is the same love Jesus offered and still does today.

Build trust

Therefore encourage one another and build each other up… – 1 Thessalonians 5:11, NIV

If you want to help the women in your small group develop meaningful and long-lasting friendships, establish trust in the group. Trust is what helps relationships grow.

One important way to build trust is to guard your tongue and encourage other members to do the same. Scripture says, “Those who guard their lips preserve their lives, but those who speak rashly will come to ruin.” (Proverbs 13:3, NIV) In abiding by this, you can foster a place where women feel comfortable and secure.

The group should be a safe space where women can talk about their feelings, ask questions they might be too afraid to ask elsewhere, and share the innermost parts of their lives. If gossip or harsh judgment takes root, your small group is no longer considered a safe harbor for those involved. Even worse, it could hurt people or harm the larger church body.

Encourage your members to keep each other’s private lives private. Lovingly stop conversations if they turn toward gossip. Create a lesson, preferably early in the group meetings, that discusses the potential harm that can come when tongues go unguarded. When a woman knows her heart is safe in your hands and in the hands of the other members of your small group, she will begin to open up. That trust is where true sisterhood begins to grow.

Encourage authenticity

Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other that you may be healed. – James 5:16, NIV

If you want to move past surface-level pleasantries and build trust, you need to take off your mask. As a leader, the speed of the group’s intimate growth is often determined by your own level of transparency. When you are willing to share your own struggles, mistakes, and sins, you give the other women permission to do the same. Authenticity creates a ripple effect by breaking down walls of perfection that so often keep people isolated.

Encourage a culture where it’s okay not to have it all together. Remind your group that the goal isn’t to have all the answers or to present a perfect, polished life, but to show up to your gatherings exactly as you are. When you create an environment where vulnerability is met with grace rather than a lecture, you will mirror the heart of Jesus, who welcomed the weary and burdened with open arms.

Carry one another’s burdens

Carry each other’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ. – Galatians 6:2, NIV

Authentic friendship often moves beyond the living room or the church basement. While the deep conversations you have during your Bible study are the catalyst for connection, the glue that holds the group together is how you show up for each other during life’s big and even mundane moments.

Encourage members of your group to look for practical ways to serve one another outside of your scheduled meeting time. Organize a meal train for a sister who is sick, offer to watch someone’s children so she can have a moment of rest, or simply send a text of encouragement in the middle of a stressful work week.

When women see that they’re cared for in real, practical ways, their hearts will soften, and they will be more willing to engage in the deeper, spiritual aspects of the ministry.

Work toward healing

He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. – Psalm 147:3, NIV

As you strive toward depth in your small group ministry, remember that some of these women carry wounds that go deeper than a weekly study or coffee date can reach. You need to exercise patience as your members work through trauma and open up about the most guarded parts of their lives.

Seek the Holy Spirit for guidance as you plan your small group sessions. Be open to the movement of the Spirit as you allow Him to guide conversations and relationships. Ask the women in the group what topics they want to discuss and study, and be open to suggestions. You never know what hidden burdens people carry. A small group is a prime opportunity for them to explore these topics that need the most.

While you can pray and love on each other in a small group, as the leader, you may not be equipped to handle all the trauma in their lives. Part of loving your sisters well is recognizing when a burden requires a specialized level of care.

Just as you would encourage a friend with a physical ailment to see a doctor, you should be open to lovingly suggesting Christian therapy for mental and emotional health. Integrating the idea of professional counseling into your conversations helps to remove the taboo and acknowledges that God often uses the wisdom of trained therapists to help untangle all the complex parts of our mental and emotional lives.

Doing life together

Cultivating deep, Christ-centered friendship in a small group setting is a process. It requires courage to be honest, the discipline to keep confidences, and the wisdom to point each other toward both God and the practical resources He provides for healing.

As you lead, remember that you’re following in the footsteps of the greatest teacher. With His help, your small group can truly become a place where authentic friendships grow and can become a safe harbor for every woman who walks through the door.

To learn more about caring for a small group or the resources available, reach out to a Christian counselor.
